title: Two chariots
hookLine: two gods meet on a narrow road; the unrighteous won't yield and falls (Jataka 457)

lines: A ROAD WITH ROOM FOR ONE.
cards: Two chariots, nose to nose on a road with room for only one, and neither driver will back up. It could be any narrow lane on any weekday morning.
In this Jataka tale the road runs through the sky, and the drivers are gods. One is named Dhamma, righteousness. The other is Adhamma, its opposite.
Each has somewhere to be, and each expects the other to move.

teach.b: First, the meeting. In the tale, both gods travel through the world in their chariots, and one day their paths cross head on, where only one can pass. Second, the claims.
Each tells the other to get out of the way, and each makes his case. Adhamma's case is force: he is strong, and gives way to no one. Dhamma's case is his goodness, and the honor the wise give it.
Adhamma will not yield. Not an inch. He even offers to fight for the road.
Dhamma's answer, in the tale's last verse between them, is that if Adhamma really is the stronger, he'll swallow the harsh words and make way for him.

At the very moment Dhamma says it, Adhamma topples from his chariot headfirst, and the earth opens and swallows him. Fourth, the road goes on. Dhamma, the Bodhisatta in this tale, continues on his way.
He never rams the other chariot or wins by shoving harder.

The one who insists on never yielding is the one who falls, and the road opens for the one who was willing to give it up. Some readers find the whole point in that fall: what cannot bend at all eventually breaks.
On an ordinary road, letting someone go first costs a few seconds; in a family argument, a little pride. The tale suggests refusing can cost a great deal more.
Yielding here isn't weakness, and it isn't losing. It's how the road stays open.

how: Dhamma, the Pali form of the Sanskrit dharma, is one of the Three Jewels Buddhists take refuge in, together with the Buddha and the Sangha.

o: a tale where the one who won't yield falls
a war between two kings of Benares
a race between two gods across the sky

p: its opposite, who won't give way

s: the two chariots meet on a narrow road in the sky
two gods, head on, with room for only one to pass.
Dhamma wins by ramming Adhamma off the road
Adhamma refuses to yield and falls from his own chariot.
Adhamma's claim to the road rests on force
he says he is strong and gives way to no one.

games.q: you're Adhamma, nose to nose with Dhamma on a road with room for one, and neither of you will move. what do you do?
o: back up and let him pass.
games.why: in the tale Adhamma refuses to yield. when Dhamma says he'll bear the harsh words and make way, Adhamma falls headfirst from his chariot.

practice: Find somewhere in the body that's braced, shoulders, jaw or hands: that's the body refusing to give way. Breathe out, and let it yield a little.
Then picture one place you'll meet someone head on, a doorway, a merge on the road, a conversation that tends to dig in, and see yourself letting them go first.

wordCard.voice: Two chariots. A Jataka tale: righteousness and its opposite meet on a narrow road, and the one who will not yield is the one who falls. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: dhamma, the teaching, what is right; in this tale it is also the name of the righteous god.

carryVoice: Your line: yielding wins. Adhamma never moved, and never got through. Day eight hundred thirty-six, done.
